The function of the turbine rotor in a heavy‑duty gas turbine engine includes carrying turbine blade loads, transmitting torque to the compressor and generator for power generation, as well as supplying the turbine blades with cooling air. Prior to assembly, the individual disks or wheels are balanced by the addition of weights installed in a groove. The weights are held in place by deforming the metal on either the balance weight or the balance weight groove. The turbine blades are retained axially by a snap‑ring type lock wire that is located in a machined groove passing through the turbine blades and turbine wheel. The portion of the wheel retaining the lock wire is known as the lock wire tab. The F‑class turbine blade cooling air supply is provided through cooling slots in the bottom of the stage 1 and 2 turbine wheel dovetails.
*Description: A cross‑section diagram illustrates a wheel mechanism with labeled components like balance weight, cooling slot, and wheel post.*

The disks in the turbine rotor are made of a high nickel alloy that is sensitive to surface imperfections where an intergranular crack may initiate and propagate due to high stresses and temperatures. Depending on the initiation location, an undetected crack may continue to propagate due to exposure to stress and temperature until either: 1‑ the crack is detected and either repaired or the rotor is removed from service, or 2‑ the crack propagates to a critical length, releasing a wheel section and/or adjacent turbine blades into the turbine hot gas path section potentially resulting in significant damage. Continuous improvements have been made to the turbine rotor wheels over time in order to improve their overall damage sensitivity.

Rotors operating in high ambient and humid or corrosive conditions have an increased risk of crack initiation and propagation. Recommended inspections and inspection intervals to mitigate crack propagation are provided based on wheel features, such as shot peening condition at first fire, cooling slot geometry, material heat treatment, and environmental conditions. In some cases, rotors may be swapped from site to site in order to expedite an outage. This TIL is being issued to all users in high ambient and/or corrosive environmental conditions in order to provide recommendations for the various configurations.

Early generation turbine rotors have the highest sensitivity to surface imperfections. These rotors were manufactured and fired without full shot peen coverage of the turbine wheels. Shot peening leaves a residual compressive stress and decreases the risk of initiating a crack. Wheels that operated without shot peening have an increased risk of initiating and propagating a crack in the rim region of the turbine rotor and in the turbine wheel dovetail slots. After 1996, all F‑class turbine wheels shipped with full peening coverage; these wheels were never fired without shot peening.

During operation, the intersection of the cooling slot and dovetail slot is subjected to high temperatures and tensile stresses caused by turbine blade pull. The high temperatures and stresses in conjunction with an adverse edge condition have been known to initiate cracks in this location.
*Figure 2: Crack at Broached Wheel Post and Original Cooling Slot Corner*
*Description: A red arrow points to a visible crack on a metallic, curved surface with a circular opening.*

Three cooling slot shapes exist including original, contoured, and enhanced. The contoured (released in 2002) and enhanced (released in 2006) cooling slot shapes were developed to lower stresses in the region where indications have been observed in original slot configuration wheels. Please see Tables 1 and 2 below for eddy current inspection recommendations for original, contour, and enhanced cooling slot configuration wheels. Some rotors may have a combination of enhanced, contoured, and/or original configuration wheels, depending on rotor repair history. All wheels should follow their applicable inspection recommendations. If a cooling slot crack is detected during the inspection, immediate wheel replacement will be recommended to help avoid the risk of wheel post liberation during operation.

Lock‑wire tab (LWT) cracks have also been detected on the turbine rotor wheels. These types of cracks can typically be repaired on site, subject to repair limits, without the need for rotor disassembly or wheel replacement.

Lock‑wire tab cracks may form in the upper corner of the lock‑wire tab groove, as shown in Figure 4. Cracks in this corner may be caused by either:
- Damage sustained during turbine blade installation/removal
- High stresses in the lock‑wire fillet

GE Vernova has developed specialized procedures and tooling to help mitigate the risk of damage to the wheel lock‑wire tabs during turbine blade installation and removal. These operations should always be performed by GE Vernova turbine blade technicians to ensure the appropriate blade installation and removal tools and techniques are utilized. Modified or back‑cut turbine blades reduce turbine blade loading into the tab. Wheels manufactured today have the extra fir trees removed in order to avoid turbine blade loading in the tab altogether, as shown in Figure 5.

Cracking has been observed on several rotors at the balance weight groove (BWG) during routine inspections (Figure 6). It has been found that this cracking initiated at an adverse edge condition because of the variability in the balance weight retention method or at a location where the wheel surface was affected by an assembly or disassembly process that may have locally altered the stress state. Cracks in the forward wheel web, if left unaddressed, could result in a partial wheel material liberation, particularly when located on the stage 1 wheel.

- If original: FPI every HGPI while buckets are removed

A visual inspection of all exposed turbine rotor surfaces is recommended for all non‑shot peened rotors; however, it is a good practice for all users to evaluate the surface of their rotor when available. In order to complete a visual inspection, observe and borescope all of the accessible rotor surfaces. Specifically, look for overall surface conditions such as dents, dings, nicks, scratches, crack‑like indications, raised material, etc.
- Broach slot fillets, slot bottoms, tangs, and cooling slots (Visual)
- Turbine blade cooling slots in wheel broach slots (Visual/BI)
- Balance weights: looseness/migration, staking quality, tight set screw (Visual/BI)
- Nut damage or surface indications in flanges and webs (BI)
- Counterbore outside diameter ligaments on distance piece and turbine aft shaft (UT)

Fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) is recommended to detect cracks on balance weights and lockwire tabs. However, it is not recommended for the wheel posts, as cracks under the dovetail tangs are typically closed.
- Staked balance weight grooves: at all major inspection intervals and when the CDC is removed during a Hot Gas Path inspection.
- Lock wire tab fillets: When turbine blades are removed during routine maintenance intervals.

If crack‑like indications are found, please contact your local GE Vernova service representative for disposition. In most cases, an in‑situ repair procedure can be used to remove cracked lock wire tabs or balance weight stake marks. A few isolated instances have occurred where wheel replacement was necessary as the repair limits were exceeded.

GE Vernova has developed an ECI method with advanced detection devices and techniques for turbine dovetail inspection (Figure 8). This method is currently the most effective non‑destructive test (NDT) for identifying indications in the wheel dovetails.

Dovetail ECI should be performed until rotor retirement at the frequency defined in Table 1. ECI is available and recommended for all wheel posts identified in Table 1 and 2. Third stage wheel posts and turbine wheels with any cooling slot configuration may also be inspected with the same equipment, if elected.

Prior to the ECI, the turbine rotor must be appropriately cleaned to facilitate proper functioning of the ECI equipment and accurate readings. A preferred method for cleaning is by dry ice (CO₂) blasting. This cleaning typically requires a single 12‑hour shift to clean the rotor after turbine blade removal and also requires the surfaces be free of oil beforehand. In the event that CO₂ blast is not available, a more arduous and lengthy hand‑cleaning process is acceptable (2‑3 shifts). The rotor inspection then takes approximately three shifts (~32 hours) to complete Stages 1 and 2. Both the rotor cleaning (performed by qualified vendor) and the turbine rotor inspection can be scheduled through your local GE Vernova representative.

The potential for crack initiation at the cooling slot location and lock wire tabs can be improved by reducing the amount of turbine blade load passing through this area of the wheel. GE Vernova has developed a turbine blade modification to change the load distribution in the wheel post, thereby decreasing the stress level at the cooling slot. This modification is accomplished by machining a tapered relief into the turbine blade dovetail pressure faces adjacent to the cooling slot (see Figure 9). Relief cut modifications have been incorporated into new production F‑class turbine blades.

The function of the turbine rotor in a heavy‑duty gas turbine engine includes carrying turbine blade loads, transmitting torque to the compressor and generator for power generation, as well as supplying the turbine blades with cooling air. Prior to assembly, the individual disks or wheels are balanced by the addition of weights installed in a groove. The weights are held in place by deforming the metal on either the balance weight or the balance weight groove. The turbine blades are retained axially by a snap‑ring type lock wire that is located in a machined groove passing through the turbine blades and turbine wheel. The portion of the wheel retaining the lock wire is known as the lock wire tab. The F‑class turbine blade cooling air supply is provided through cooling slots in the bottom of the stage 1 and 2 turbine wheel dovetails.

The disks in the turbine rotor are made of a high nickel alloy that is sensitive to surface imperfections where an intergranular crack may initiate and propagate due to high stresses and temperatures. Depending on the initiation location, an undetected crack may continue to propagate due to exposure to stress and temperature until either:
1. the crack is detected and either repaired or the rotor is removed from service, or
2. the crack propagates to a critical length, releasing a wheel section and/or adjacent turbine blades into the turbine hot‑gas path section potentially resulting in significant damage.

Continuous improvements have been made to the turbine rotor wheels over time in order to improve their overall damage sensitivity.

Rotors operating in high ambient and humid or corrosive conditions have an increased risk of crack initiation and propagation. Recommended inspections and inspection intervals to help mitigate crack propagation are provided based on wheel features, such as: shot peening condition at first fire, cooling slot geometry, material heat treatment, and environmental conditions. In some cases, rotors may be swapped from site to site in order to expedite an outage. This TIL is being issued to all general F‑Class turbine rotors in order to provide recommendations for the various configurations. Rotors operating in high ambient and/or corrosive conditions have an increased risk of crack initiation and propagation and are addressed in TIL 1937.

Early generation turbine rotors have the highest sensitivity to surface imperfections. These rotors were manufactured and fired without full shot peen coverage of the turbine wheels. Shot peening leaves a residual compressive stress and decreases the risk of initiating a crack. Wheels that operated without shot peening have an increased risk of initiating and propagating a crack in the rim region of the turbine rotor and in the turbine wheel dovetail slots. After 1996, all F‑class turbine wheels shipped with full peening coverage; these wheels were never fired without shot peening.

During operation, the intersection of the cooling slot and dovetail slot is subjected to high temperatures and tensile stresses caused by turbine blade pull. The high temperatures and stresses in conjunction with an adverse edge condition have been known to initiate cracks in this location.

Three cooling slot shapes exist including original, contoured, and enhanced. The contoured (released in 2002) and enhanced (released in 2006) cooling slot shapes were developed to lower stresses in the region where indications have been observed in original slot configuration wheels. Please see Tables 1 to 6 below for eddy current inspection recommendations for original, contour, and enhanced cooling slot configuration wheels. Some rotors may have a combination of enhanced, contoured, and/or original configuration wheels, depending on rotor repair history. All wheels should follow their applicable inspection recommendations. If a cooling slot crack is detected during the inspection, immediate wheel replacement will be recommended to avoid the risk of wheel post liberation during operation.

Prior to the ECI, the turbine rotor must be appropriately cleaned to facilitate proper functioning of the ECI equipment and accurate readings. A preferred method for cleaning is by dry ice (CO₂) blasting. This cleaning typically requires a single 12‑hour shift to clean the rotor after turbine blade removal, and also requires the surfaces be free of oil beforehand. In the event that CO₂ blast is not available, a more arduous and lengthy hand‑cleaning process is acceptable (2‑3 shifts). The rotor inspection then takes approximately three shifts (~32 hours) to complete Stages 1 and 2. Both the rotor cleaning (performed by qualified vendor) and the turbine rotor inspection can be scheduled through your local GE Vernova representative.

The potential for crack initiation at the cooling slot location and lock wire tabs can be improved by reducing the amount of turbine blade load passing through this area of the wheel. GE Vernova has developed a turbine blade modification to change the load distribution in the wheel post, thereby decreasing the stress level at the cooling slot. This modification is accomplished by machining a tapered relief into the turbine blade dovetail pressure faces adjacent to the cooling slot (see Figure 9). A gas turbine rotor is an assembly of shafts, wheels, disks, and spacers. A means of balance is incorporated into each of these rotor components and the various assemblies. A balance weight groove (BWG) is one example of a feature that is used to provide a means of balancing. The BWG is an annular channel that is machined into a rotor component that provides a location for weights to be installed for balance purposes on either the piece part or as a rotor assembly. This annular channel may contain two BWG entry slots, as shown in Figure 1, located approximately 180 degrees apart that allow for the balance weights to be easily installed and located in the appropriate locations on the wheel or shaft.

During non‑destructive evaluation (NDE) of a distance piece (DP) as part of a rotor life extension (RLE), a crack‑like indication was observed in the corner of a balance weight groove entry slot. Both grooves on the specific part showed similar indications as depicted in Figure 2. GE has inspected additional parts with similar features and observed similar indication findings.
**Figure 2: Indications Found on DP During RLE – Observed Machining Issue**

Upon completion of a root cause investigation, GE determined the cause is associated with the variation in the corner condition of the balance weight groove entry slots and interactions with the various stresses during gas turbine start‑up, shutdown, and loaded operation (gravity sag, etc). Depending upon the specific nature of a unit’s operation and the specific condition of the part slot corner, crack‑like indications may form over the lifetime of the component. If these crack‑like indications propagate to a large enough size, it may be possible for continued rapid crack growth to occur associated with gravity sag related bending of the rotor as it rotates (high cycle fatigue related mechanism). If not mitigated, the fracture propagation may lead the CAS and/or DP to separate into two separate pieces. Separation of either shaft into two pieces may create the possibility for components to exit the gas turbine leading to the possibility for INJURY TO PERSONNEL/INDIVIDUALS and substantial damage to adjacent equipment.

Equivalent cold rotor turning time is defined as a spinning rotor in combination with cool metal temperatures (generally speaking conditions with all wheelspace temperatures measuring less than 150 degrees F). Turning gear (TG) operation, forced cooling operation, offline water wash operation, and unit startups are the periods where cool rotor conditions exist and contribute to the overall equivalent cold rotor turning time. Equivalent refers to a standardization of the # of high cycle fatigue cycles for a given hour and therefore has a component associated with the accumulation of cycles relative to the rotor speed. For example, at purge speed (~20% speed) versus turning gear speed (~6 rpm) a higher # of stress cycles will occur per minute of operation due solely to the increased rotational speed of the rotor for a given period.

The compressor section of F‑Class gas turbines has 18 (0‑17) stages of rotating components (rotor blades) and stationary components (stator vanes).

Some F‑class machines have experienced aft end compressor rubs. These rubs range from light scoring on the casing to material loss at the blade tip. This phenomenon was concluded to be very low risk relative to unit operation and reliability. No performance impact and no forced outages have been experienced as a result. Rotor blades in rows 13, 14, and 15 are primarily affected.

To inform users to monitor equipment operation and condition, and to identify the onset, occurrence, and effects of aft‑end compressor rubs (when the tip of the rotor blade rubs the casing). Rubs are evident when blade tip material is adversely affected. Information in this TIL is supplemental to information in the Inspection and Maintenance Manual provided with the gas turbine.

Based on the conclusion of Root Cause Analysis (RCA) and fleet experience, aft end rubs are primarily induced because of frequent restarts between two (2) to eight (8) hours after shutdown. During this transient period, the thermal compression of the casing relative to the rotor can decrease clearances and can lead to rubs upon restart. The heat generated from a rub can lower the local material fatigue strength of the blade resulting in material tip loss in the event of another rub. Typical material loss dimensions are less than 1/16 inch² in area (see Figure 2).

Restarting a unit 2 to 8 hours after a shutdown or trip is within the operating envelope, but this may cause rubs in some cases. Aft end rubs and/or tip loss pose very low risk to unit operation and reliability. No performance impact and no forced outages have been experienced due to this issue.

Follow operating practices per GER 3620 to reduce the potential for rubs on aft end compressor blades. In addition to the GER 3620 guidelines, the following recommendations would also help minimize aft end rubs and tip loss occurrence.
- Keep enclosure doors closed during startup, shutdown and normal operation.

- Be aware that restarting the gas turbine between two (2) and eight (8) hours following a shutdown or trip will cause the clearances in the aft end to decrease. If the unit operates this way now or has in the past, there is a potential for this clearance closure to cause aft end tip rubs. As a result, the area should be included in the yearly borescope inspections.
- Eliminate any potential pipe leaks that may cause quenching of the gas turbine compressor discharge casing.
- Ensure vent fans and exhaust fans to the gas turbine enclosure are functioning properly such that no local forced convection is taking place at or near the compressor discharge casing.

- Integrate the inspection for aft end compressor rubs with your yearly scheduled borescope inspection per GER 3620. Observe rotor blade stages 13 through 17 and look for mushroomed material (see Figure 3), bluing at the blade tip, and / or markings in the casing area.

As the forward‑most rotating blade in an F‑class gas turbine compressor, the R0 (Rotor stage 0 blade) is the first to see airborne materials ingested through the inlet (see Figure 1). In addition to solid objects that may create immediate and substantial impact damage, ingested fluids and liquid droplets may also affect the blades, though more gradually, accumulating erosion primarily along the leading edge of the R0 (see Figure 2).

Common sources of water ingested through the gas turbine compressor inlet during operation include OnWW, fogging/SPRITS system output, and evaporative cooling system carry‑over. Water ingestion could also result from unintended sources such as the leakage of rainwater through compromised inlet ducting seals or malfunctioning accessory equipment.
[Figure: Crowd image] (A large crowd of people is densely packed together, viewed from a high angle.)

Leading edge erosion degrades the blade's material capability by creating a dense network of surface pits (see Figure 3) and has resulted in compressor event forced outages, with cracks initiating from erosion pits at the root of the R0 airfoil.

Failure to follow these recommendations could result in excessive erosion, which, in turn, could lead to subsequent cracking and possible liberation of R0 blades with potential downstream damage to the gas turbine.

Recommendations for monitoring erosion levels caused by known sources of potential water droplet introduction to the inlet air stream are given in the following section. The recommended method for erosion quantification is through mold impressions and GE Power Services provides a process for evaluating these molds. The accumulation of erosion may at some point require leading edge surface renewal prior to reaching a degradation limit. Compressor fouling results from the depositing of airborne contaminants onto the compressor flow path surfaces and it affects a decline in aerodynamic efficiency and, thus, gas turbine performance. Water washing of the compressor is necessary to reduce the fouling effects and maintain a desired level of output. However, water washing performed on‑line inherently injects water droplets into the compressor at a high relative velocity, thereby creating a source of R0 leading edge erosion.

TIL 1323 advises performing a modification to the original online water wash system to reduce the volume of water impinging on the R0 leading edge root location (the area susceptible to cracking from erosion). With this modification, erosion rates are improved, but still require special maintenance intervals. GE has now engineered and validated a new online water wash system that imparts significantly reduced erosion at the R0 root and requires no maintenance for up to 1000 cumulative hours of washing. This allows for daily water washing (15 minutes per 48 fired hours) with no R0 erosion maintenance necessary until the scheduled Major Inspection interval. The new configuration has been validated through accelerated field testing which confirmed the reduced rate of erosion while maintaining the same cleaning effectiveness as the baseline system. The system has been introduced into GE F‑class production as well as retrofitted into field units as a system upgrade. Contact your GE Power Services representative for information on this upgrade.

## For current F‑class units operating with the original OnWW system (which should be modified per TIL 1323), erosion levels should be inspected at regular intervals of OnWW by taking mold impressions of the R0 leading‑edge root location.  See “Combined Wet Inlet Operation” for inspection interval information.  Contact your GE Power Services representative to arrange this inspection.  Mold inspections should be followed by fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) to ensure against existing cracks.

OnWW should be performed based on desired output degradation limits as well as environmental effects to the forward compressor. When fouling deposits contain corrosive elements, washing can help minimize corrosive attack.
### General guidelines for OnWW duration and frequency are as follows:
- 5 minutes per 48 Fired Hours, if standard R0's and the Gen‑1 WW system are in place
- 15 minutes per 48 Fired Hours, if standard R0's and the Gen‑2 WW system are in place (available through CM&U)
- 15 minutes per 48 Fired Hours, if enhanced R0s (ECP 2, 2+3, 4, 5) are installed with either the Gen‑1 WW or the Gen‑2 WW system

These durations are advised to balance erosion rates and output degradation. Shorter durations or longer intervals between washing may be scheduled at the operator’s discretion based on minimal performance degradation or corrosion concerns. Conversely, longer or more frequent water washes could result in a greater rate of erosion, requiring more frequent repairs. For this reason, the upgraded OnWW system now available generally limits daily washes through control system permissives.

Water carry‑over into the compressor may originate from inlet fogging systems. These systems introduce water droplets into the air stream that may coalesce and contribute to R0 leading edge erosion. Erosion rates will vary based on spray ratio, maintenance practices and operating frequency.

For units utilizing fogging systems, GE recommends that R0 blades be inspected with mold impressions and FPI at regular intervals of cumulative hours of fogger operation as defined in “Combined Wet Inlet Operation”.

Though evaporative cooler systems are intended to cool the air and introduce moisture (not water droplets) for increased mass flow and efficiency, inadvertent water carry‑over from this system may affect R0 erosion. GE recommends monitoring the evaporative coolers for proper operation and any evidence of water carry‑over. This evidence may include water stains, puddles, or streaking in the filter inlet house or bell mouth area; deposits on filter or cycle deck material; or missing, damaged, or misaligned filter or cycle deck material.

Any evidence of water carry‑over should be dispositioned and eliminated by GE or the manufacturing vendor. Refer to TILs 1285 and 1399 for additional information on evaporative cooler maintenance and annual commissioning.

R0 erosion molds and FPI should be performed between 100 and 300 hours of cumulative operation of the evap system. For units with identified water carry‑over, the inspection should be repeated at this interval or as determined based on the mold impressions. If there is no significant erosion and it is continually verified that the evap system is generating no carry‑over, no continual R0 mold inspection is necessary.

Many operators may use a combination of water‑introducing systems. R0 erosion inspections should include both mold impressions and FPI and should be performed when cumulative wet inlet operation time reaches 100 hours as defined by the following formula:
Combined Wet Time = 4 × (OnWW hours [A]) + 0.1 × (OnWW hours [B]) + (Fogger hours [C]) + 0.2 × (SPRITS hours [D]) + (Evap hours [E])

Where [A] pertains to the legacy OnWW system, [B] pertains to the upgraded OnWW system, [C] applies for non‑GE foggers, [D] applies for GE fogging/SPRIT'S systems, and [E] applies only if carry‑over has been present or the evaporative cooler system has not been commissioned or maintained per TILs 1285 and 1399.

From this, it can be seen that if an upgraded OnWW system is applied and evaporative coolers have been commissioned and maintained, then recurring mold inspections are primarily dependent on the accumulation of Fogging/SPRITS operation. These systems may have significant variability based on manufacturer, vintage, system tuning and modifications. As such, following initial inspections, parameters C and D may be adjusted per GE disposition (see Figure 5).

It should be anticipated that wet inlet operation will result in some level of R0 erosion for which the disposition could be a reduced interval for subsequent inspection or even discontinuance of further wet inlet operation until the R0s can be blend repaired by qualified GE Energy Services technicians. Blade repairs performed by GE Services may be conducted in‑situ; however, with a seed set of R0s, removal and repair in a GE Service Center will often minimize outage delays.
